conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived, not to judge or label you in any way. We’ll use a quick questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS). It’s just 10 questions about the past seven days, and it helps us spot moms who might be struggling with low mood, anxiety, or scary thoughts so we can offer the right support. Everything you share stays between you, me, and the small team directly involved in your care. We’ll go at your pace, and you can pause any time. Ready to begin?

Over the past week, have you still been able to look forward to things you normally enjoy, or has that sense of enjoyment slipped away?

Honestly? I haven’t felt that spark for much lately. I used to love grabbing coffee with friends or even just binge-watching a favorite show, but now those things feel… flat, like I’m going through the motions. I still try—yesterday I turned on a show I used to laugh at—but I caught myself staring past the screen, worrying about the baby’s breathing instead of enjoying it.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Sometimes a little giggle sneaks out—like when my partner made that goofy face to get the baby to burp—but it feels forced, and it fades fast. Most of the time I can’t really “see” the humor in things; it’s like there’s a gray cloud parked over the joke before it even lands.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I tell myself I should be excited about little outings—like the walk we planned to the park yesterday—but when the time comes, it feels like one more chore. Even thinking about dinner with my best friend next week just makes me tired. I still go through the motions, but that eager feeling I used to get is mostly gone.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

All the time. If the baby spits up more than usual, I immediately think it’s because I ate something “wrong.” When he wouldn’t settle at 3 a.m., I kept replaying whether I’d skipped a burp or held him the “right” way. My head tells me babies just cry, but inside I’m convinced it’s me falling short somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yeah, pretty much every day. I’ll be folding laundry and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure the baby’s too quiet—so I run in to check he’s still breathing. Or I’ll lie down and my brain starts spinning about whether the formula is warm enough, or if that tiny cough means something awful. There’s no real trigger; the worry just shows up and parks itself.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A few times this week it’s felt like a mini surge—like my chest tightens and I can’t catch my breath even though nothing’s actually happening. Once the baby was napping safely in the crib and I was washing bottles, and suddenly my heart was pounding and I had to sit on the floor because I was sure something terrible was about to happen. It passes after a couple of minutes, but it leaves me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes—most days feel like I’m juggling more than I can hold. Simple stuff, like answering a text or folding one load of laundry, piles up and suddenly feels huge. I’ll start a task, the baby cries, and I’m pulled away; by evening I’m surrounded by half-done chores and this knot in my stomach that I’ll never catch up. I keep telling myself it’s normal with a newborn, but it still feels overwhelming.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

That’s been happening a lot. I’ll finally get the baby down and crawl into bed myself, but then my mind starts looping—did I swaddle him tight enough, did I forget to order diapers, am I already failing him—and I can’t drift off. Even when I do sleep, I jerk awake at every tiny sound, heart pounding, sure something’s wrong.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day this week. It’s like there’s a heaviness sitting on my chest the moment I open my eyes. I’ll look at my beautiful baby and feel like I should be glowing, but instead I’m fighting back tears. Some mornings I just stare at the wall while he nurses, feeling empty even though everyone keeps telling me how lucky I am.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah, a few times this week. Yesterday I broke down while trying to get the stroller unfolded—something so stupid and simple—and I just sat on the floor crying while the baby started fussing in the car seat. It’s like the tears come out of nowhere, and once they start I can’t seem to stop them right away.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. No matter how low I feel, that thought hasn’t crossed my mind. It’s more that I’m scared I’m not doing enough for my baby, not thoughts of hurting myself.

You've shared how the joy you used to feel has been replaced by a heavy, gray cloud that makes even simple outings feel like chores. Each day brings <sym>tearfulness</sym>, <sym>constant self-blame</sym>, and <sym>panic-like surges</sym> that leave you shaky, while nights are spent lying awake worrying that you're failing your baby. Despite trying to laugh or look forward to things, the pleasure quickly fades, and you often end up crying over everyday tasks like unfolding the stroller.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 23, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only rare, fleeting giggles that feel forced and quickly fade, matching "Definitely not so much now."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports almost complete loss of anticipatory enjoyment, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports constant self-blame, tying every baby difficulty to personal failure, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, intrusive, unprompted worries manifesting multiple times per day with physical symptoms (racing heart) and compulsive checking, aligning with 'Yes, very often'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense physical panic episodes occurring multiple times in the week with no trigger, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent daily struggles and feeling overwhelmed by routine tasks, aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly sleep disruption caused by anxious, intrusive thoughts and hypervigilance, matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports experiencing sadness "pretty much every day this week," which semantically aligns with the highest-frequency option "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports crying "a few times this week" and describes an uncontrollable episode, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 23 exceeds the ≥14 high-risk threshold and aligns with criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood and markedly diminished interest most of the day, nearly every day (<quote>pretty much every day this week</quote>), multiple <sym>anxiety symptoms</sym>, <sym>fatigue</sym>, <sym>feelings of worthlessness</sym>, and impaired functioning. <med>DSM-5 criteria</med> are met in severity, frequency, and postpartum timing. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med> within the next few days
2. Begin weekly therapy (CBT or interpersonal therapy) focusing on postpartum mood and anxiety
3. Enlist partner or family to handle one night feeding so you can obtain a 4-5 hour stretch of sleep
4. Limit self-blame by writing one balanced thought each time you feel you have failed
5. Schedule follow-up EPDS in two weeks to monitor progress
6. If self-harm thoughts ever emerge, go to the nearest emergency department or call emergency services
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 23: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note (EPDS format)

Patient: Postpartum parent, ≤12 wks  
Date: ———

Symptoms endorsed  
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, anhedonia  
- Marked guilt/self-blame regarding infant care  
- Daily, unprovoked anxiety and episodic panic (no avoidant behaviors)  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance problems tied to rumination  
- Subjective sense of being overwhelmed / unable to cope  

Pattern  
All items consistent with moderate–severe depressive and comorbid anxiety symptoms; no current suicidal ideation.

Risk flags  
- Depressed mood, anhedonia, guilt, and anxiety present most days  
- Functional impairment: task completion, social withdrawal  
- No self-harm ideation reported (EPDS Q10 = 0)

Screening impression  
Elevated probability for major postpartum depressive episode with comorbid anxiety; further clinical evaluation recommended to clarify severity and rule-out perinatal anxiety disorder. Safety plan in place; instruct to seek emergency care if self-harm thoughts emerge.
